5 words · live is 4 · “Our First 90 Days” is the one weak element in an otherwise excellent section. It says nothing about the page, it implies the company is 90 days old, and there is no 90-day period anywhere in the copy beneath it. Margo has been manufacturing for over two decades.

leads: What we have never done is write any of it up.
marked: **What we have never done is write any of it up.** We have no published case studies, and we would rather say so than manufacture one. This page exists because we believe our first documented partners deserve to know exactly what to expect before they decide to work with us, not after.
fields.note:
50 words · live is 33 · this is the most important edit on the page and it is one added clause.
The live sentence is true and it is read as something else. “We do not yet have documented export case studies” is heard by a first-time buyer as we have no export track record — and one click away, /about publishes a 24-name client wall across seven sectors. A buyer who sees both pages does not conclude that Margo is modest; they conclude that one of the two pages is wrong.
“What we have never done is write any of it up” separates the two facts and it changes the page from we are new to we have a long record and have never documented it. Only the second is accurate, and it is the more persuasive of the two

sections.title: Methodology preview
sections.chip: 4 cards stay four · two stats corrected
sections.live: LIVE H2 → What Our Case Studies Will Cover · a genuinely good four-stage structure · two of the four stat chips contradict the rest of the site

fields.label: Eyebrow · H2

lines: What Our Case Studies Will Cover

fields.note: [no change to either]

fields.label: Intro
paragraphs: When we publish our first documented case study, it will follow this four-part structure. We are sharing the format now so prospective buyers understand the rigour behind what we will report — and what you can hold us accountable to.
marked: When we publish our first documented case study, it will follow this four-part structure. We are sharing the format now so prospective buyers understand the rigour behind what we will report — and what you can hold us accountable to.
fields.note: 39 words · live is 39 · comma fixed to a dash. “What you can hold us accountable to” is the best clause on this page and it should never be edited out

fields.label: Card 01 — Challenge

parts.text: Every case study begins with the exact component brief — tolerances, material grade, application environment and regulatory requirements. We document what the buyer needed, and why a standard off-the-shelf part fell short.

fields.note:
32 words · live is 33 · the stat chip is the correction. The homepage, /about and /products publish ±0.01 mm; this card publishes ±0.05 mm. Two tolerance claims on one website, and neither is a real specification.
±0.01 mm is a misreading of the company profile, where the figure is the resolution of the measuring instrument. And no moulded rubber part carries a single blanket tolerance — it varies with dimension, geometry and shrinkage, which is exactly what ISO 3302-1 exists to express. Naming the class is what a buyer’s drawing will call out anyway

fields.label: Card 02 — Component Specced

parts.text: We record the compound chosen, the mould geometry, shore hardness and the rationale. Buyers see exactly how the specification maps to the final formulation.

fields.note:
24 words · live is 32 · the parenthetical list comes out of the body — “(EPDM, NBR, Silicone, Neoprene, etc.)” names four of eight and then abbreviates, which reads as a sample of many rather than most of a short list.
The stat chip is the real correction. The homepage table publishes eight compounds and every product page in this set is written against those eight. 20+ against 8 is not rounding — a buyer who counts the table concludes one of the two numbers is padding, and on a page whose entire argument is we do not embellish, that is the most expensive place on the site to be caught rounding up.
“Published in full” is the stronger claim anyway. Most competitors will not tell you the compound at all

fields.label: Card 03 — QC Process

parts.text: Each case study will log the inspection checkpoints — hardness testing, compression set to ASTM D395 Method B, tensile strength and dimensional verification — against the agreed acceptance criteria.

fields.note:
29 words · live is 27 · the standard number is added to the body — the tests named are all on Margo’s published list, and naming the method for one of them is what separates a checklist from a capability.
The label is a scope correction. Certificate 09111526A covers rubber moulded components; extrusion and sponge/foam sit outside it. “Every batch” is not true of two of the eleven product categories, and an auditor checking the certificate scope will find that in under a minute

fields.label: Card 04 — Outcome Metrics

parts.text: We will report lead time met against lead time committed, rejection rate at final inspection, on-time delivery, and any post-delivery feedback. Numbers, not adjectives.

rows: Batch traceability from compound to despatch

fields.note: 24 words · live is 26 · “Numbers, not adjectives” is the best three-word sentence on this website. It is the whole editorial position of this content set, written by the client, before anyone reviewed the site. Set it in bold and leave it alone

notes: Stage titles are <h3>. The 01–04 numerals are decorative — put them in a <span aria-hidden="true">, not in the heading text, or every heading on the page starts with a digit.

This section is the page’s AEO asset and it is unusual. “What should a rubber component case study contain?” and “how do you verify a moulded rubber part?” have almost no good published answers. A four-stage method with a named test in stage 3 is exactly the shape an answer engine lifts whole.
ISO 3302-1 named in text. It is the string a buyer’s drawing carries and it appears nowhere on this site today.
Do not put the stat chips in images. They are the section’s only figures.
No ItemList schema. A described process is not a list of published works.

paragraphs: Hardness ranges, temperature profiles and chemical resistance for all eight compounds we mix — AEM, FKM, NBR, EPDM, silicone, neoprene, SBR and natural rubber — published on the page, not gated behind a form.

35 words · live is 33 · the button changes from a download that does not exist to a page that does.
“Published on the page, not gated behind a form” is worth saying out loud. It is true, it is unusual in this sector, and it is the same argument as “numbers, not adjectives” one section above — which makes the page consistent with itself. Never ship a control with no destination. Three on this page today. A dead button is a soft 404 — invisible to a crawler, obvious to a buyer, and on this page it directly refutes the argument the page is making.

paragraphs: If you place a trial order with us, we will publish a full case study on this page — with your approval — that documents the process from specification to delivery. No embellishment. No invented outcomes.
marked: If you place a trial order with us, we will publish a full case study on this page — with your approval — that documents the process from specification to delivery. No embellishment. No invented outcomes.

33 words · live is 28 · one clause changed, and it is the same fix as the hero.

The rest of the paragraph is untouched

No Offer or Review schema. An invitation to be documented is not a product offer and there is no review to mark up.

This section is the page’s best chance of being cited by name. “Which manufacturers publish honest case studies?” is a question with almost no good answers, and a supplier that states it has none is a genuinely novel passage.
Do not A/B test this section into something softer. Its whole value is that it says something no competitor page says.

notes: What it fixes on this page specifically: the footer CTA promises a quotation “within 24 hours” while section 05, 763 px above it, promises “within one business day”. Two response commitments in one document, on the one page whose entire argument is that Margo does not overstate. The footer is where the sitewide constant lives, so fixing it here fixes it on all forty pages at once.

And the second contradiction on the same page: the footer description claims supply “across 50+ countries” while the homepage claims 95. A page that says numbers, not adjectives cannot carry two different numbers for the same fact.

What it fixes on this page specifically: the footer carries the correct phone number and email — the two strings the CTA two sections above it publishes as placeholders, This page does not carry the placeholder CTA variant that HVAC, electrical & electronics, agriculture and water do — its closing CTA is the plain shared block, so the footer is the only place contact details appear. They are correct here.

The Products column must show all eleven — and lining makes twelve. It currently shows nine. This page links to /products once, from section 03, so the footer is the only place a case-studies visitor sees the category list at all. Rubber sheet lining is client-confirmed (2026-09-02) and has no category, no page and no footer entry — the largest single gap in the site’s product structure.

Build once, ships forty times. This is one component. The copy above is written out in full on every sheet in this set so nobody has to open two files to build one block, but it is authored once in the codebase.

Link equity. 26 sitewide links from here. Adding /export, /products/extrusion and /products/sponge-foam-rubber gives three orphaned or under-linked URLs a sitewide inbound link each — the cheapest internal-linking win available on this site.
NAP markup. Wrap in <address>. Phone as <a href="tel:+919665579276">, email as <a href="mailto:info@margorubber.in">. The visible string and the href must not diverge.

Schema. The footer emits nothing. The Organization node on the homepage is the single entity definition and every other page @id-references it. Repeating an Organization block per page creates 40 competing entities.
Copyright year. Render from new Date().getFullYear(), not a literal. It has read 2024 for eight months.
